opus-5.5.text:
I think math is a uniquely good training ground, and the reason is verification. In most domains, when a model produces an answer, it's hard to know for sure whether it's right. In mathematics, especially formal mathematics with something like Lean, you get a proof checker that tells you with certainty whether every step holds. That gives you a clean, scalable reward signal, which is exactly what you want for reinforcement learning and self-improvement.

What generalizes isn't the theorems. It's the reasoning habits. To prove something hard, a system has to plan over long horizons, break a big problem into lemmas, notice when an approach is failing and backtrack, and build abstractions it can reuse later. Those are the same capabilities you need for writing complex software, designing experiments, or reasoning through an engineering system. Math compresses all of that into a setting where you can actually measure progress.

There's also a very direct bridge to code. A formal proof is a program. Lean is a programming language. So the skills of producing verified mathematics transfer naturally to producing verified software, and that matters a lot as AI writes more of the world's code. If you can trust a proof, you can start to trust critical systems in chip design, cryptography, aerospace, and finance.

I'd add one caveat. Math alone won't give you general intelligence. The real world is messy, ambiguous, and often lacks a clean verifier. But I see math as a kind of anchor. It's where we can push reasoning to its limits in a rigorous way, learn how to build systems that genuinely discover new things rather than just recall, and then carry those methods into domains where verification is softer. Historically, math has been the language underneath physics, computer science, and much of engineering. I think AI for math can play a similar foundational role for AI more broadly.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the honest answer starts with why mathematics is such a special testbed in the first place. It's the one domain where we have a verifier. If a model produces a proof in Lean, the kernel tells you whether it's correct, full stop. There's no human in the loop grading it, no ambiguity about whether the answer was "good enough." That gives you a clean reward signal, and clean reward signals are the thing that lets you scale reinforcement learning without the model learning to flatter the grader instead of actually getting better.

So the first thing math gives you is a laboratory. We can study how reasoning capability actually improves when you have ground truth, and then ask which of those lessons transfer to domains where you don't.

The second thing, and I think this is underappreciated, is that mathematics is the compression of reasoning itself. Formal proof forces you to make every step explicit, to handle every case, to never hand-wave. A model that gets genuinely good at this is learning something about rigor and long-horizon planning that is not really about numbers or algebra. It's about holding a very long chain of dependencies in your head and knowing when a step is justified. That skill shows up in software verification, in physics, in chip design, anywhere you need correctness over a long horizon rather than plausibility over a short one.

Where I'd push back on the easy version of this story is the assumption that it generalizes automatically. I don't think it does. A model that is superhuman on competition problems can still be quite bad at formulating the right question, and in the real world the question is usually the hard part. Mathematicians spend most of their time deciding what's worth proving. So the path to something more general isn't just "solve harder theorems." It's building systems that can go from a vague, messy human intention to a precise formal statement, work on it, and then translate back. That round trip, informal to formal to informal, is where I think most of the generalization actually lives.

And if you take that seriously, math becomes less of a destination and more of an engine. We build the rigor and the verification stack in the domain where we can measure it, and then we deliberately widen the aperture: science, engineering, eventually any domain where you can build even a partial verifier. Every time you can turn fuzzy judgment into something checkable, the math machinery starts to apply. That's the version of "AI for math leads to general intelligence" that I actually believe in. Not that solving math makes you generally smart, but that learning to make reasoning verifiable is a skill the rest of the world badly needs.

astra-6.text:
I think mathematics is a useful testing ground for general intelligence because it combines reasoning with a way to check whether that reasoning is correct. You can explore an idea, get feedback, and revise your approach. That makes it a powerful setting for learning.

But the interesting question is what transfers beyond math. Can a model learn to break a difficult problem into smaller pieces, find a useful abstraction, or recognize when its current approach is going nowhere? Those abilities matter in science, engineering, and many other domains.

I wouldn’t assume that getting very good at proving theorems automatically produces general intelligence, though. Outside mathematics, problems are often underspecified, evidence is incomplete, and there may not be a single correct answer. So I see AI for math as a route toward developing and testing some of the ingredients of general intelligence. The next challenge is making those ingredients work when the world doesn’t give you a clean proof checker.

sol-6.1.text:
I think mathematics is a useful testing ground for general intelligence because it requires more than knowing facts. You have to choose an approach, break a problem into smaller pieces, recognize when you’re stuck, and sometimes invent a new way to represent the problem. Those abilities matter far beyond math.

What makes math particularly useful is that you can often check whether the reasoning actually works. That gives you a feedback signal for training systems to reason over longer horizons. The hope is that the habits they learn—forming conjectures, testing ideas, revising a plan—can transfer to science, engineering, and other kinds of discovery.

But I wouldn’t assume that being excellent at mathematics automatically gives you general intelligence. The real world has ambiguous goals, incomplete information, and questions where there isn’t a clean right answer. So the interesting question is whether a system learns a general process for discovering things, or becomes very good at solving problems within a particular formal setting. I see AI for math as a promising route toward that broader capability, with transfer still something we need to demonstrate.
